name: Pizza
description: A flatbread of yeast dough baked in a hot oven under tomato sauce, cheese and toppings until the crust blisters and crisps. Born in Naples, it is now one of the most recognisable dishes on earth, with endless local variations on what goes on top.
fact: The Margherita is widely said to be named after an Italian queen, its red, white and green echoing the national flag.

name: Sushi
description: Vinegared rice paired with raw fish, seafood or vegetables, pressed by hand or rolled. Japan knows dozens of forms, from nigiri to maki, and the whole idea began as a way of preserving fish by packing it in rice.
fact: The word sushi refers to the vinegared rice rather than the fish, which is why a sushi can be entirely vegetarian.

name: Burger
description: A bun holding a griddled beef patty with cheese, vegetables and sauces, the backbone of fast food almost everywhere. It took its modern shape in the United States around the turn of the twentieth century and became a national culinary emblem.
fact: The name hamburger comes from the German city of Hamburg, whose emigrants carried the recipe for minced beef patties abroad.

name: Carbonara
description: Pasta in a sauce of egg, hard cheese, guanciale and coarse black pepper, with no cream at all in the classic Roman version. The silkiness comes from beaten eggs setting in the residual heat of the pasta, never from simmered cream.
fact: Where the name comes from is still argued over; one story ties it to charcoal burners who supposedly lived on the dish up in the hills.

name: Pasta bolognese
description: Pasta with a slow ragù of minced beef, tomato, soffritto vegetables and wine, cooked down for hours until it turns deep and glossy. The Bolognese original is traditionally served not with spaghetti but with broad ribbons of tagliatelle.
fact: In Italy ragù is rarely put on spaghetti; tagliatelle is considered the proper partner for it.

name: Lasagna
description: Sheets of pasta layered with meat or vegetable sauce, béchamel and cheese, then baked until the top browns and bubbles at the edges. The dish comes from Emilia-Romagna and counts among the oldest forms of pasta in Italy.
fact: Layered pastry dishes very like lasagna already appear in fourteenth-century cookery manuscripts, both Italian and English.

name: Risotto
description: Rice cooked slowly in broth, stirred constantly while the liquid goes in ladle by ladle, until the grains release their starch into a creamy whole. One of the best-known versions is risotto alla milanese, turned gold by saffron.
fact: Risotto needs short-grain varieties such as arborio, which give up enough starch to produce that creamy texture.

name: Ravioli
description: Small squares or rounds of thin pasta sealed around a filling of meat, cheese or vegetables, boiled and served with a sauce. Cousins of the dumplings eaten the world over, they are thoroughly Italian, with a history reaching into the Middle Ages.
fact: Ravioli fillings were once often made from yesterday's leftover meat, so that nothing went to waste.

name: Gnocchi
description: Little dumplings, most often of potato, flour and egg, boiled briefly and dressed with butter, tomato sauce or pesto. Dough dumplings of this kind existed in Europe long before the potato ever reached an Italian kitchen.
fact: In Rome gnocchi are traditionally eaten on Thursdays, a habit some trattorias still keep to.

name: Bruschetta
description: A thick slice of bread grilled over the fire, rubbed with garlic, doused in olive oil and piled with a topping, most classically tomatoes and basil. A plain central-Italian starter that has travelled around the world.
fact: The name comes from the Italian verb bruscare, meaning to roast over coals.

name: Caprese
description: Slices of tomato and mozzarella layered with basil leaves and finished with olive oil. Red, white and green, the colours of the Italian flag, on a plate whose recipe is traced to the island of Capri.
fact: It is traditionally served without vinegar or extra flourishes: the flavour rests entirely on the quality of three ingredients.

name: Minestrone
description: A thick vegetable soup bulked out with beans, pasta or rice, changing completely from region to region and season to season. The name comes from minestra, simply soup, and captures the point of the dish: cook what you happen to have.
fact: There is no single recipe for minestrone; practically every Italian family makes its own version.

name: Tiramisu
description: Layers of savoiardi biscuits soaked in coffee, bound with a mascarpone cream and dusted with bitter cocoa. The name means "pick me up", a nod to the jolt of caffeine that the coffee and cocoa deliver at the end of a meal.
fact: Tiramisu is thought to have been invented in the Veneto only in the second half of the twentieth century, making it a very young dessert.

name: Panna cotta
description: A delicate set cream of dairy, sugar and gelatine, turned out of its mould and served with berry or caramel sauce. The name means "cooked cream", though the mixture is only warmed through and never brought to the boil.
fact: Piedmont is the usual claim for its birthplace, and before gelatine was available the cream was thickened with isinglass.

name: Gelato
description: Italian ice cream churned with less air and less fat than the industrial kind, which makes it denser and more intense in flavour. It is served a little warmer than ordinary ice cream, so the texture stays soft and spoonable.
fact: Gelato is usually made and kept at a higher temperature than standard ice cream, and that alone changes its texture.

name: Cannoli
description: Crisp tubes of fried dough filled with sweetened ricotta, often studded with candied peel or shards of chocolate. A Sicilian pastry that became famous worldwide largely thanks to the Italian diaspora in the United States.
fact: A line about cannoli in The Godfather became one of the most quoted remarks about Sicilian food.

name: Carpaccio
description: Raw beef or fish sliced paper-thin, dressed with olive oil and lemon juice and often scattered with parmesan and rocket. Invented in Venice in the middle of the twentieth century and named after a painter fond of reds and whites.
fact: The dish is named for Vittore Carpaccio, whose canvases share the colour of raw beef.

name: Ramen
description: Wheat noodles in a deep broth built on meat, fish or miso, topped with egg, sliced pork and vegetables. The dish arrived in Japan from China and over the decades grew into a culture of its own, with countless regional styles.
fact: Japan has entire museums devoted to the history of ramen, and every region keeps its own signature broth.

name: Udon
description: Thick, chewy wheat noodles served hot in broth or cold with a sauce for dipping. One of the oldest noodle types in Japan, particularly beloved in the Sanuki area of Shikoku, where the local style has its own devoted following.
fact: The thickness and soft bite of udon make it the most instantly recognisable Japanese noodle, by texture as much as by taste.

name: Miso soup
description: A light soup of dashi stock stirred through with miso paste, with cubes of tofu and wakame seaweed floating in it. One of the fixtures of a traditional Japanese breakfast or lunch, set on the table alongside almost any other dish.
fact: Miso paste is made by fermenting soybeans, and the ageing can run from a few months to several years.

name: Tempura
description: Seafood and vegetables dipped in a thin batter and deep-fried until the coating turns lacy and crisp. Portuguese missionaries brought the technique of frying in batter to Japan back in the sixteenth century, and it became thoroughly Japanese.
fact: The lightness of tempura depends on ice-cold batter and barely mixing it, so that no gluten develops.

name: Yakitori
description: Pieces of chicken threaded onto bamboo skewers and grilled over charcoal, usually glazed with a sauce of soy and mirin. The word means "grilled bird", and in a good yakitori bar every part of the chicken finds its way onto a skewer.
fact: Traditional yakitori places use almost the whole bird, cartilage and skin included, so that nothing is thrown away.

name: Onigiri
description: Triangles or rounds of pressed rice, usually wrapped in a band of nori, with something tucked inside: salmon, pickled plum or seaweed. Portable food sold on practically every corner in Japan, from station kiosks to convenience stores.
fact: Onigiri were being made centuries ago as easy provisions for travellers and warriors, food that survived a journey.

name: Gyoza
description: Dumplings of minced pork and cabbage, seasoned with garlic and ginger, either pan-fried or steamed. They came to Japan from China and were reworked for local taste, ending up with thinner wrappers and a crisp browned base.
fact: Classic gyoza are fried so that one side turns crunchy while the dough on top stays soft from the steam.

name: Takoyaki
description: Round balls of batter with a piece of octopus in the middle, cooked in a special pan of hemispherical moulds and turned with a skewer. Osaka street food, served hot under sauce and mayonnaise with a snow of bonito flakes.
fact: The name comes from tako, octopus, which remains the one indispensable ingredient.

name: Sashimi
description: Raw fish or seafood sliced thin and served without rice, unlike sushi, usually with soy sauce and wasabi. Everything rests on the freshness of the fish and on the knife skill that shapes each slice.
fact: The Japanese name translates literally as "pierced body" and refers to the way the fish is cut.

name: California roll
description: An inside-out sushi roll with the rice on the outside, filled with crab, avocado and cucumber and usually rolled in tobiko. It was invented not in Japan but in the United States, as a sushi without raw fish for Western diners.
fact: The California roll is considered one of the first sushi rolls created specifically for a Western audience.

name: Philadelphia roll
description: A sushi roll of salmon, cream cheese and cucumber, named after the American brand of cream cheese that goes into it. Another case of Japanese cooking rebuilt for Western palates, well outside Japan itself.
fact: For all its Japanese styling, the Philadelphia roll was an invention of American sushi bars in the late twentieth century.

name: Poke
description: A Hawaiian dish of raw fish cut into cubes, most often tuna, marinated in soy sauce and served over rice with vegetables. What began as plain fishermen's food has turned into a bowl format popular around the world.
fact: Poke means "to cut into pieces" in Hawaiian, which is exactly how the fish for it is prepared.

name: Taco
description: A corn or wheat tortilla folded over a filling of meat, vegetables and salsa. One of the best-known things to eat on a Mexican street, and it exists in dozens of regional guises, from grilled fish to slow-braised pork.
fact: Tacos al pastor are cut from a vertical spit, a method brought to Mexico by immigrants from the Middle East.

name: Burrito
description: A large wheat tortilla wrapped tightly around meat, rice, beans and vegetables into a dense cylinder. Mexican in origin, though the burrito as it is eaten today was largely shaped north of the border, in the United States.
fact: The word burrito means "little donkey", perhaps because a rolled tortilla resembles a pack strapped to the animal's back.

name: Quesadilla
description: A tortilla filled with cheese, folded in half and griddled until the outside is golden and the inside molten. Meat, vegetables or mushrooms often join the cheese, and it comes to the table with guacamole or sour cream.
fact: The classic quesadilla is built around melted cheese, queso in Spanish, which is where the name comes from.

name: Nachos
description: Crisp corn tortilla chips generously drowned in melted cheese and often loaded with meat, vegetables and sauces. The dish was invented in a Mexican border town in the middle of the twentieth century and named after the man who thought of it.
fact: It carries the name of a cook nicknamed Nacho, who put it together for a group of customers in the 1940s.

name: Guacamole
description: A dip or paste of mashed avocado with onion, lime, coriander and chilli, served with chips or spooned alongside other dishes. The recipe goes back to the Aztecs, long before any European set foot in Mexico.
fact: The name comes from the Nahuatl ahuacamolli, which means literally "avocado sauce".

name: Fajitas
description: Strips of beef seared with onion and bell pepper, brought to the table still sizzling in the pan with warm tortillas so that everyone builds their own. The dish belongs to Tex-Mex, the border cooking of Mexico and Texas.
fact: Fajitas began with a cheap cut of beef, the skirt, and that is where the name comes from: faja, a strip or belt in Spanish.

name: Chili con carne
description: A thick stew of minced beef, beans, tomato and hot chilli pepper, simmered slowly until the flavour deepens. For all the Mexican roots of its name, the dish in its present form took shape in Texas.
fact: Texas itself holds official chili con carne cook-offs that go back decades.

name: Churros
description: Ridged strips of dough deep-fried until crisp, rolled in sugar and usually served with a cup of thick hot chocolate for dipping. Street food and breakfast alike across Spain and Latin America.
fact: One story has it that the shape of churros imitates the horns of the mountain sheep that Spanish shepherds kept.

name: Pad thai
description: Rice noodles stir-fried with egg, soy and fish sauce, often with prawns or chicken, finished with crushed peanuts and bean sprouts. The Thai government actively promoted the dish in the mid-twentieth century as an emblem of the national kitchen.
fact: Pad thai spread through a state campaign that, among other things, taught Thais to eat more noodles and less rice.

name: Tom yum
description: A hot and sour Thai broth with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves and chilli, most often with prawns in it. Outside Thailand it is one of the most recognisable things the country's cooking has produced.
fact: The name joins two Thai words: tom, meaning to boil, and yam, a hot and sour spiced salad.

name: Tom kha
description: A Thai soup on a base of coconut milk with chicken, galangal, lemongrass and mushrooms, milder and creamier than tom yum. The coconut milk rounds off the heat of the spices, leaving the soup gentle but still fragrant.
fact: Though it shares its spices with tom yum, tom kha owes its particular flavour to the coconut milk.

name: Pho
description: A Vietnamese soup of rice noodles in a fragrant broth of beef bones, star anise and cinnamon, with slices of meat and a handful of fresh herbs. One of the pillars of Vietnamese cooking, eaten at breakfast, lunch and dinner alike.
fact: The name pho may come from the French pot-au-feu, a dish that influenced Vietnamese cooking in the colonial period.

name: Spring rolls
description: Thin rice wrappers rolled around vegetables, herbs, rice noodles and sometimes prawns or pork. They come either fresh, with a dipping sauce alongside, or deep-fried until the wrapper turns brittle and golden.
fact: Fresh Vietnamese spring rolls, unlike the fried kind, need no cooking at all once they are rolled.

name: Bánh mì
description: A Vietnamese sandwich in a crackling baguette, packed with pâté, pickled vegetables, fresh herbs and meat. It sets the French legacy of the colonial years against thoroughly Vietnamese flavours and spices.
fact: The thin, crisp baguette that holds a bánh mì is a direct inheritance from the French colonisation of Vietnam.

name: Nasi goreng
description: Rice fried with sweet soy sauce, vegetables, egg and meat or prawns, usually crowned with fried shallots and served with prawn crackers on the side. One of the most popular dishes in Indonesia, cooked in practically every household.
fact: The name means simply "fried rice", and every family and every region of Indonesia makes it differently.

name: Satay
description: Marinated pieces of meat on skewers, grilled over charcoal and served with a thick sauce of roasted peanuts. Eaten all over Southeast Asia and especially loved in Indonesia and Malaysia, where it is sold on every street.
fact: The peanut sauce for satay is made with spices and lemongrass, which gives it a rich, sweet and faintly fiery taste.

name: Laksa
description: A spicy noodle soup built either on coconut milk or on a sour broth, at home in Malaysia and Singapore. It brings Chinese and Malay cooking together, which is why it is called the emblematic dish of Peranakan culture.
fact: There are many regional versions of laksa, and they can differ markedly in colour, heat and the make-up of the broth.

name: Dim sum
description: Small plates of steamed dumplings, buns and rolls, brought to the table in little baskets over the course of a long Chinese tea meal. They grew out of Cantonese cooking and became the heart of the ritual known as yum cha.
fact: Eating dim sum is bound up with drinking tea: the term yum cha means literally "to drink tea".

name: Peking duck
description: Duck with crisp, lacquered skin, roasted by a particular method and served thinly sliced with thin pancakes, spring onion and hoisin sauce. One of the most celebrated dishes in Chinese cooking, with centuries of history behind it.
fact: To get the skin crisp, the duck is scalded with boiling water and then air-dried, sometimes for a full day.

name: Kung Pao chicken
description: Pieces of chicken stir-fried with peanuts, dried chillies and vegetables in a hot, slightly sweet sauce. The dish comes from Sichuan, and its name goes back to the title of an official at whose table it was supposedly first served.
fact: The name comes from the honorific gong bao, held in the nineteenth century by a governor of Sichuan.

name: Fried rice
description: Rice tossed over a fierce flame with egg, vegetables and often meat or prawns, made from rice that has already been boiled and left to cool. One of the most widespread dishes in Chinese cooking, with dozens of regional versions.
fact: Yesterday's slightly dried rice is held to fry best; freshly cooked rice is too wet and clumps together.

name: Wontons
description: Delicate dumplings of thin dough filled with minced pork or prawn, served floating in broth or deep-fried. The wrappers are rolled especially thin, which is what sets wontons apart from the sturdier Chinese jiaozi.
fact: In English-speaking countries wonton soup became one of the most familiar dishes on a Chinese restaurant menu.

name: Baozi
description: Fluffy steamed buns of yeasted dough filled with meat, vegetables or sweet paste. They are eaten with the hands, often at breakfast or as a snack, and they cook in stacked bamboo steamer baskets.
fact: The soft, airy dough of baozi comes from a yeast starter and a long proving before the buns go into the steamer.

name: Kimchi
description: Fermented vegetables, most often napa cabbage, seasoned with red pepper, garlic and ginger. One of the great emblems of Korean cooking, set out on the table at practically every meal of the day.
fact: South Korea has dedicated refrigerators designed for nothing but storing and fermenting kimchi.

name: Bibimbap
description: Rice topped with assorted vegetables, meat, an egg and hot gochujang paste, served in one bowl and stirred together before eating. The name means literally "mixed rice", and the dish is famous for its bright array of colours and flavours.
fact: The hot version arrives in a scorching stone bowl, which turns the rice at the bottom crunchy.

name: Tteokbokki
description: Cylinders of chewy rice cake simmered in a sweet and fiery sauce based on gochujang pepper paste. One of the most popular street foods in South Korea, particularly beloved by schoolchildren and students.
fact: Tteokbokki is often sold from street carts alongside fish cakes and boiled eggs, dropped straight into the sauce.

name: Chicken tikka masala
description: Pieces of chicken marinated in spices and yoghurt, cooked in the oven and served in a thick, spiced sauce of tomato and cream. Although the dish is associated with India, the Indian diaspora in Britain played a large part in its making.
fact: Some food historians hold that the modern tikka masala recipe was worked out by Indian cooks in Britain.

name: Butter chicken
description: Chicken in a mild, creamy sauce of tomato, butter and spices, gentler than most Indian curries. It was devised in Delhi in the middle of the twentieth century as a way of using up leftover tandoori chicken.
fact: The story goes that the sauce was invented to keep tandoori chicken from drying out: leftover meat was stirred into tomato and butter.

name: Biryani
description: A layered dish of long-grain basmati rice, meat or vegetables and a blend of spices, brought together in a sealed pot over a low fire. Regional versions run all over India and Pakistan, each with its own set of spices.
fact: The rice and the meat are often cooked separately, then layered and finished together in the steam of a sealed pot.

name: Naan
description: A soft yeasted wheat flatbread, traditionally baked against the wall of a clay tandoor oven. It arrives hot at the table alongside curry and other Indian dishes, often brushed with butter or scattered with garlic.
fact: The shaped dough is slapped straight onto the searing inner wall of the tandoor, where it bakes in a couple of minutes.

name: Samosa
description: Triangular parcels of thin pastry stuffed with potato, peas and spices, deep-fried until the shell crackles. A snack across South Asia and the Middle East, bought from street stalls or eaten with afternoon tea.
fact: The ancestor of the samosa is thought to have reached India with Persian and Central Asian traders back in the Middle Ages.

name: Curry
description: A blanket name for dishes in a thick, spiced sauce, made with meat, fish or vegetables. Recipes and spice blends differ sharply from region to region: there is no single thing called "curry" in India at all.
fact: The word curry entered English from the Tamil kari, which means a sauce or gravy.

name: Borscht
description: A hearty soup built on beetroot, which gives it its deep red colour, together with cabbage, potato and meat. Eaten all over Eastern Europe, and traditionally served with sour cream and garlic pampushky rolls.
fact: In 2022 UNESCO added the culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking to its list of intangible heritage in urgent need of safeguarding.

name: Pelmeni
description: Small parcels of thin unleavened dough filled with minced meat, boiled in water or in broth. They count among the emblems of Russian cooking, though many peoples across Eurasia have something very similar of their own.
fact: In Siberia pelmeni were traditionally made in huge batches and frozen outdoors to last the whole winter.

name: Blini
description: Thin pancakes of a loose batter, fried in a pan and served with sour cream, butter, caviar or a sweet filling. One of the oldest dishes in Russian cooking, tied closely to the Maslenitsa carnival and the welcoming of spring.
fact: At Maslenitsa a round golden pancake traditionally stood for the sun and for seeing winter off.

name: Olivier salad
description: A salad of boiled vegetables, meat or sausage, eggs and pickled cucumbers, bound with mayonnaise. It was invented in the nineteenth century by a cook of French origin, though today's version has drifted a long way from the original recipe.
fact: Lucien Olivier's original recipe is said to have contained grouse and crayfish tails, and he kept it a secret.

name: Herring under a fur coat
description: A layered salad of salted herring, potato, carrot and beetroot under mayonnaise, named for the bright "fur coat" of the top layer. A fixture of New Year and festive tables across the former Soviet Union.
fact: The popular claim that the "fur coat" is an acronym of a revolutionary slogan was invented in our own day: the beetroot layer simply looks like one.

name: Vinegret
description: A salad of boiled beetroot, carrot and potato with pickled cucumber and sauerkraut, dressed with sunflower oil. The name comes from the French vinaigrette, although the dish itself took shape within Russian cooking.
fact: All that is left of French cooking here is the name of the dressing; the salad itself was put together in Russia.

name: Shchi
description: A soup of fresh or fermented cabbage with meat or mushrooms, one of the oldest and most revered soups in Russian cooking. In winter thick shchi was often frozen and taken on the road, hacked off in chunks and reheated at a halt.
fact: An old Russian saying paired shchi with kasha as "our food", which shows how central the soup was to the everyday diet.

name: Okroshka
description: A cold soup of finely chopped vegetables, boiled meat and eggs, flooded with kvass, kefir or whey. It is made and eaten in summer, a dish meant to cool you down when the heat leaves no appetite for anything else.
fact: Classic okroshka is made with bread kvass, though versions on kefir are increasingly common today.

name: Solyanka
description: A thick, robust soup built on pickled cucumbers, olives and lemon, with several kinds of meat, fish or sausage in it. The brine and the sheer variety of ingredients give it a striking sour, salty and sharp flavour.
fact: There are meat, fish and mushroom versions of solyanka, united by the same sour and salty character of the broth.

name: Ukha
description: A clear fish soup boiled from one or several kinds of fish with the barest handful of vegetables, so that nothing drowns out the taste of the fish. One of the oldest dishes in Russian cooking, bound up with fishing and camp traditions.
fact: To make the broth especially clear, whisked egg white was sometimes added to ukha, gathering up the cloudiness.

name: Beef Stroganoff
description: Thinly sliced beef, seared and then simmered in a sour cream sauce, often with mustard and onion. The dish is named after the aristocratic Stroganov family and has been travelling well beyond Russia since the nineteenth century.
fact: The dish carries the Stroganov name, though the exact story of how it came about is still disputed.

name: Chicken Kiev
description: A flattened chicken breast wrapped around a piece of butter, breadcrumbed and fried until golden. Cut it open and the hot butter runs out, which is what makes serving this dish such a small piece of theatre.
fact: Despite the name, some accounts of its origin tie the dish not to Kyiv at all but to the French culinary tradition.

name: Kholodets
description: Meat stock set to a jelly with pieces of meat in it, simmered for hours until the bones and cartilage give up enough gelatine to set on their own. Served cold, usually with horseradish or mustard, and above all at a festive table.
fact: To set without added gelatine, the stock is boiled for a very long time using the parts of the carcass richest in collagen.

name: Pirozhki
description: Small pies of yeasted or unleavened dough with all kinds of fillings, from potato and cabbage to meat and berries, either fried or baked. Homely, universal baking, found all across Eastern Europe.
fact: Whether pirozhki are fried or baked, and the shape they take, traditionally depends on the region and the family.

name: Syrniki
description: Small fried cakes of curd cheese, egg and flour, served for breakfast with sour cream, jam or honey. In spite of the name, no cheese goes into them: the base is curd, which some Slavic languages call cheese anyway.
fact: The name is explained by history: in some East Slavic languages curd cheese was simply called "cheese".

name: Varenyky
description: Parcels of unleavened dough filled with potato, curd cheese, sour cherries or cabbage, boiled in salted water. One of the great emblems of Ukrainian cooking, and familiar in many other countries of Eastern Europe too.
fact: The closest relatives of varenyky are Polish pierogi: both are crescents of unleavened dough, pinched shut by hand.

name: Cabbage rolls
description: Cabbage leaves rolled around a filling of minced meat and rice, then braised in a tomato or sour cream sauce. The dish is eaten across Eastern Europe and the Balkans, though recipes and the way it is served differ noticeably.
fact: The technique is close to dolma, the stuffed vine leaves known across the Balkans and the Middle East.

name: Draniki
description: Pancakes of grated raw potato, fried in a pan until the edges crisp, usually served with sour cream. One of the mainstays of Belarusian cooking, and known under other names in Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine as well.
fact: Similar potato pancakes turn up in many European kitchens, among them Jewish latkes and German Kartoffelpuffer.

name: Medovik
description: A tall cake of thin honey layers spread with sour cream or custard, left to stand before serving so that the layers soften into one another. Legend has it that it was invented for a Russian empress who could not stand the smell of honey.
fact: Honey goes into the dough together with baking soda: the reaction lightens it, makes it rise and lends a caramel tone.

name: Napoleon cake
description: A tall cake of crisp puff pastry layers spread with custard, popular right across the former Soviet Union. The name points to the French mille-feuille, though the recipe as it is baked today took shape in Russia.
fact: In Russia the name is linked to the centenary of the victory over Napoleon, though the recipe has no direct connection to the emperor.

name: Shashlik
description: Chunks of marinated meat threaded onto metal skewers and grilled over the coals of a mangal. Especially popular in the Caucasus and in Russia, where it is cooked at picnics and holidays almost all year round.
fact: The word shashlik came into Russian from Crimean Tatar and is related to shish, a spit.

name: Pilaf
description: Rice, meat, carrot and onion cooked together in a cauldron so that the grains soak up the fat and the juices of the meat. Regional versions run through Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Middle East, each with its own rules.
fact: In Uzbekistan pilaf is often the centrepiece of a large celebration, and recipes and technique differ noticeably from city to city.

name: Manti
description: Large parcels of thin dough filled with hand-chopped meat and onion, steamed in a special multi-tiered pot. They are eaten all over Central Asia, the Caucasus and Turkey under closely related names.
fact: The classic filling is chopped with a knife rather than put through a mincer, which keeps the meat juicy.

name: Laghman
description: Long noodles pulled by hand, served with a rich meat and vegetable gravy, either soupy in a bowl or thick enough to count as a main course. A favourite of the Uyghurs and eaten right across Central Asia.
fact: Masters spend years learning to pull laghman dough by hand into long, even threads.

name: Samsa
description: Flaky pastries filled with meat, onion and spices, traditionally baked against the walls of a tandoor until the crust turns golden and crisp. Popular all over Central Asia, where they are often sold as street food.
fact: The name and origin of samsa belong to the same culinary tradition as the Indian samosa.

name: Beshbarmak
description: Boiled meat, most often lamb or horse, served with broad sheets of rolled noodles and a bowl of the broth. The name means literally "five fingers": the dish is traditionally eaten with the hands, from a shared platter.
fact: Beshbarmak is regarded as the principal celebration dish of the Kazakhs and other Turkic peoples of Central Asia.

name: Chebureki
description: Thin turnovers of unleavened dough filled with minced meat, deep-fried until the crust blisters and crackles. A Crimean Tatar dish that spread widely through Russia and Ukraine, sold hot from kiosks and cafés.
fact: A properly made cheburek should squirt a little hot juice at the first bite.

name: Khachapuri
description: A flatbread of yeasted dough filled with cheese, whose best-known form is the Adjarian boat with an egg and butter on top. One of the central dishes of Georgian cooking, and it exists in a whole range of regional shapes.
fact: In the Adjarian version the egg and butter are stirred straight into the hot cheese, and pieces are torn off the rim to dip.

name: Khinkali
description: Large Georgian dumplings with juicy minced meat and broth sealed inside. They are eaten with the hands, held by the twist of dough on top: you bite a small hole first and drink the broth, and the twist is usually left on the plate.
fact: In Georgia the twists left on the plate are counted to see how many khinkali each person at the table got through.

name: Kharcho
description: A hot Georgian beef soup with rice, walnuts and something sour in it, most often tkemali plums or pomegranate juice. Its depth of flavour comes from the mix of spices, khmeli suneli among them.
fact: For the sour note Georgians often use tklapi, plum purée dried into a thin sheet, which dissolves straight into the broth.

name: Chakhokhbili
description: Chicken braised with a great deal of onion, tomato and herbs, cooked without any added oil or water at all. It belongs to traditional Georgian home cooking and is marked by a deep, concentrated tomato flavour.
fact: Chakhokhbili was originally made with game birds, and chicken only became the standard ingredient later on.

name: Satsivi
description: A cold dish of chicken or turkey in a thick walnut sauce with spices, among them utskho suneli and Imeretian saffron. Traditionally set out on the Georgian festive table, and very often at New Year.
fact: The sauce is built on ground walnuts alone, with no flour or starch used to thicken it.

name: Lobio
description: Beans stewed with onion, garlic and herbs, brought to the table either hot or cold. One of the mainstays of Georgian fasting cooking, usually eaten with mchadi, the flat cornbread of the region.
fact: Lobio comes in dozens of versions, from hot and stewed to a cold one pressed into patties with walnuts.

name: Churchkhela
description: Nuts threaded on a string, dipped again and again in thickened grape juice and dried until the coating turns dense and chewy. A traditional Georgian sweet, made above all during the grape harvest.
fact: The coating is cooked from grape juice with flour, and the nuts are dipped many times, the layer growing and drying between dips.

name: Dolma
description: Vine or cabbage leaves rolled into small parcels around rice and often spiced minced meat. The dish is eaten across the Caucasus, the Balkans and the Middle East, where it exists in a great many versions.
fact: The name dolma comes from a Turkish word meaning "filled" or "stuffed".

name: Shawarma
description: A thin flatbread wrapped around finely sliced roast meat, vegetables and sauce. The dish rests on the technique of roasting meat on a vertical spit, used right across the Middle East and carried from there into Europe.
fact: Roasting meat on a vertical spit is the basis of a whole family of related dishes, from Turkish döner to Greek gyros.

name: Kebab
description: A blanket name for dishes of grilled meat, often on skewers or a spit, found throughout the Middle East, the Caucasus and Central Asia. The particular recipe and the way it reaches the table vary sharply from country to country.
fact: The name of the famous döner kebab means "turning kebab", after the rotating vertical spit the meat cooks on.

name: Falafel
description: Balls of ground chickpeas or broad beans with spices, deep-fried until crisp and often served in a pitta with vegetables and tahini sauce. One of the great street foods of the whole Middle East, eaten from morning onwards.
fact: Falafel is thought to have been made originally with fava beans, with the chickpea version spreading later.

name: Hummus
description: A paste of boiled chickpeas, tahini, garlic, lemon juice and olive oil, served with flatbread or raw vegetables. One of the most recognisable things in Middle Eastern cooking, and now a popular dish all over the world.
fact: The word hummus means literally "chickpeas" in Arabic, after the main ingredient of the dish.

name: Tabbouleh
description: A salad of fine bulgur wheat with a great deal of parsley and mint, tomatoes and a dressing of lemon juice and olive oil. It comes from Levantine cooking, and all that greenery gives it a fresh, herbal taste.
fact: In a classic tabbouleh there is usually more parsley than bulgur: the herbs, not the grain, are the main ingredient.

name: Shakshouka
description: Eggs baked in a thick sauce of stewed tomato, onion and pepper with spices, brought to the table in the pan itself. Popular across the Middle East and North Africa, often as a filling breakfast with bread for mopping up the sauce.
fact: The name shakshouka is linked to an Arabic word for something "mixed up", a nod to how the sauce is made.

name: Couscous
description: Fine grains of durum wheat steamed until light and fluffy, often served with stewed vegetables and meat. The foundation of traditional cooking across the Maghreb, in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, where it is made almost daily.
fact: In 2020 UNESCO added the knowledge and skills of making and serving couscous to its list of intangible heritage.

name: Tagine
description: Meat or vegetables stewed with dried fruit and spices, cooked slowly in the cone-shaped clay pot that gives the dish its name. The shape of the lid lets the steam condense and run back down, so nothing dries out.
fact: The dish takes its name from that very conical clay pot, in which it is both cooked and served.

name: Baklava
description: A layered dessert of the thinnest filo pastry packed with ground nuts and soaked in sugar or honey syrup. Eaten across the Balkans, the Middle East and the Caucasus, where the cuts and the nut fillings differ from place to place.
fact: A classic baklava takes dozens of paper-thin layers of pastry, rolled out almost to transparency.

name: Paella
description: Rice cooked in a wide, shallow pan with saffron, vegetables and either seafood or meat. It comes from Valencia, where the traditional recipe called for rabbit, chicken and beans rather than anything from the sea.
fact: Connoisseurs prize the socarrat, the browned, faintly crisp layer of rice that forms right at the bottom of the pan.

name: Gazpacho
description: A cold puréed soup of ripe tomatoes, cucumber, pepper and bread, dressed with olive oil and vinegar. The classic summer dish of southern Spain, drunk chilled when the weather turns fierce.
fact: Early versions of gazpacho had no tomatoes: that vegetable only entered the recipe after it reached Europe from the Americas.

name: Jamón
description: Cured pork ham, aged for a long stretch of time until the texture firms up and the flavour deepens. It is served in thin slices, either on its own as a starter or as an addition to other dishes.
fact: The finest jamón can be aged for several years, and the longer it hangs the richer the meat tastes.

name: Spanish omelette
description: A dense omelette of eggs and fried potato, often with onion, cooked in a pan and flipped over whole. One of the most common dishes in Spanish home cooking, served either hot or cold, at any hour of the day.
fact: The great argument among Spanish cooks is whether onion belongs in it at all, and there is no settled answer.

name: Patatas bravas
description: Cubes of fried potato served under a spicy tomato sauce and often a garlic aioli as well. One of the most popular tapas in Spanish bars, with a name that translates roughly as "fierce potatoes".
fact: The word bravas refers to the heat of the sauce poured over the potatoes, not to the way they are fried.

name: Croissant
description: Crescent-shaped laminated pastry of yeasted dough with a great deal of butter, which is what makes it crisp outside and airy within. It has become one of the chief emblems of a French breakfast.
fact: The crescent shape, by one account, goes back to an Austrian pastry that the French croissant was modelled on.

name: Ratatouille
description: A stew of aubergine, courgette, pepper and tomato with the herbs of Provence, the region the dish comes from. It can be cooked as a plain rustic stew or arranged as neat overlapping slices of vegetable.
fact: The refined version, with thinly sliced vegetables laid out in careful rows, owes much of its fame to the animated film of the same name.

name: French onion soup
description: A soup of long-caramelised onion in beef or chicken stock, served under a lid of bread and melted cheese. One of the classics of French cooking, especially welcome in the cold months of the year.
fact: The crucial part of the recipe is the long caramelisation of the onion, sometimes close to an hour, which gives the soup its deep sweetness.

name: Crème brûlée
description: A delicate custard of cream and egg yolks under a thin, brittle crust of caramel. The crust is traditionally made by scattering sugar over the custard and scorching it with a torch just before it goes to the table.
fact: A recipe under the name crème brûlée appears in a French cookbook of the late seventeenth century, so the dessert is over three hundred years old.

name: Quiche Lorraine
description: An open tart of shortcrust pastry filled with a custard of egg and cream and pieces of fried smoked bacon. It comes from Lorraine in north-eastern France, which is where the name of the dish comes from.
fact: The classic quiche Lorraine recipe contains no onion; that version is considered a later addition to the original.

name: Bouillabaisse
description: A rich fish soup of several kinds of fish and seafood with spices and saffron, from the port of Marseille. It is traditionally served with croutons and rouille sauce, and the broth and the fish are sometimes eaten in turn.
fact: Bouillabaisse began as fishermen's food, made from the unsold catch, small fish that were hard to shift at market.

name: Foie gras
description: A delicacy made from the specially fattened liver of a duck or goose, unusually soft and rich in texture. One of the best-known and at the same time most contested parts of French gastronomy, because of the way the birds are fed.
fact: Producing foie gras by the traditional method is banned in a number of countries and regions over concerns about the welfare of the birds.

name: Steak tartare
description: Finely chopped raw meat, most often beef, seasoned with capers, onion and spices, sometimes crowned with a raw egg yolk. There is a fish version of the dish as well, made with tuna or salmon.
fact: The name is linked to the Tatars, though the historical connection between the recipe and their cooking remains disputed.

name: Macaron
description: A small almond meringue biscuit in two halves, crisp on the outside and soft in the middle, sandwiched around a creamy filling. It is known for bright colours and dozens of flavours of filling.
fact: Getting a perfectly smooth shell and the characteristic "foot" on a macaron is reckoned one of the hardest tasks in pastry work.

name: Éclair
description: An oblong pastry of choux dough filled with cream, most often crème pâtissière, and glazed on top. The name means "lightning", by one account because of the speed at which it is usually eaten.
fact: Another account ties the name to the glossy glaze on the pastry, which is said to recall a flash of lightning.

name: Profiteroles
description: Small balls of choux pastry filled with cream or ice cream, usually served under a chocolate sauce. Profiteroles are also stacked into a celebration tower, held together with threads of caramel.
fact: A tower of profiteroles bound with caramel is traditionally served at French weddings in place of a cake.

name: Fondue
description: Cheese melted with white wine and garlic in a communal pot, into which pieces of bread go on long forks. A traditional dish of the Alpine regions of Switzerland and France, eaten in company around one table.
fact: There is a sweet version too: chocolate fondue, for dipping fruit and pieces of cake.

name: Raclette
description: A dish of melted cheese scraped straight onto boiled potatoes, pickles and cured meats. The name comes from the French verb racler, to scrape, which describes exactly the way it is served at the table.
fact: Raclette is at once the name of the cheese, of the dish, and of the special device that melts it at the table.

name: Wiener schnitzel
description: Veal beaten thin, coated in breadcrumbs and fried in plenty of fat until the crust turns golden and crisp. One of the chief emblems of Austrian cooking, and by tradition it has to be made from veal and nothing else.
fact: In Austria there are firm views on the matter: a real Wiener schnitzel is veal, never pork.

name: Bratwurst
description: A German sausage of pork or veal with spices, either fried or boiled, served with mustard and bread or in a roll. Dozens of regional versions of the recipe exist across Germany, each region certain of its own.
fact: Some German regions have strict rules governing the recipe and even the size of the local bratwurst.

name: Pretzel
description: A twisted enriched bread in its distinctive knotted shape, dark and glossy outside and soft within, dipped in an alkaline solution before it is baked. One of the chief emblems of Bavarian and German food culture.
fact: The pretzel has long served as the guild sign of bakers, and it still turns up on bakery signs in Germany today.

name: Apple strudel
description: A roll of the thinnest stretched pastry filled with apple, cinnamon, raisins and nuts, baked until the crust is golden and crisp. One of the great desserts of Austrian and central European cooking.
fact: The pastry for a real strudel is stretched by hand so thin that, as the saying goes, you could read a newspaper through it.

name: Goulash
description: A thick soup or stew of beef with onion, paprika and potato, simmered slowly until the flavour deepens. It began as shepherds' food and became one of the chief emblems of the Hungarian national kitchen.
fact: It is paprika, which only became widespread in Hungarian cooking in the nineteenth century, that gives goulash its red colour and its taste.

name: Fish and chips
description: Fish in a crisp batter, deep-fried and served with thick-cut fried potatoes. One of the most recognisable things in British street food, traditionally handed over wrapped in paper and eaten straight from it.
fact: The dish was so widespread in Britain that during the Second World War it was left out of the rationing system.

name: Full English breakfast
description: A substantial breakfast of fried eggs, bacon, sausages, grilled tomatoes, mushrooms, baked beans and toast. A traditional plateful served in British pubs and cafés all day long, not only in the morning.
fact: Scotland and Ireland add their own elements to this breakfast, such as potato scones or soda bread.

name: Shepherd's pie
description: A bake of stewed minced meat under a layer of mashed potato, browned in the oven. The name points to the lamb traditionally used in the filling, as opposed to the beef version, which is called cottage pie.
fact: Bakes like this were originally made from leftover roast, with the layer of mash standing in for pastry.

name: Hot dog
description: A sausage in a bun split along its length, finished with mustard, ketchup, onion and whatever else is going. One of the great emblems of American street food, bound up with baseball stadiums and sidewalk carts.
fact: The name hot dog, by one account, grew out of a joke about the sausage's resemblance to a dachshund.

name: French fries
description: Potatoes cut into slim batons and deep-fried until crisp, often twice over, first at a low temperature and then at a high one. Despite the English name, they are associated first of all not with France but with Belgium.
fact: In Belgium they are sold from dedicated friteries and handed over in a paper cone, most often with mayonnaise.

name: Ribeye steak
description: A cut of beef from the rib section, shot through with veins of fat that keep the meat juicy as it cooks. One of the most popular steak cuts, thanks to a deep flavour and a tender texture that forgives a little imprecision on the grill.
fact: The veins of fat that make a ribeye so juicy are called marbling, and they have a direct effect on the taste.

name: Barbecue ribs
description: Pork or beef ribs cooked long and slow over low smoke, often finished with a sweet and spicy barbecue sauce. The dish is tightly bound to the cooking traditions of the American South, where several distinct regional styles grew up.
fact: Different American states have fundamentally different barbecue styles, differing in the sauce and in how the meat is smoked.

name: Fried chicken
description: Pieces of chicken dipped in spices and flour or batter and deep-fried until the crust crackles. One of the cornerstones of Southern cooking in the United States, and later the foundation of a global fast food chain.
fact: Southern fried chicken recipes go back to traditions brought both by European settlers and by enslaved Africans.

name: Buffalo wings
description: Chicken wings deep-fried and coated in a hot sauce of cayenne pepper and butter, served with blue cheese dip and celery sticks. The dish was invented in a bar in Buffalo, New York, which is where the name comes from.
fact: Buffalo itself holds an annual festival devoted entirely to chicken wings and the sauces that go with them.

name: Mac and cheese
description: Macaroni in a thick cheese sauce, often baked afterwards until the top browns. One of the homeliest and most recognisable dishes in American cooking, loved by children and adults in equal measure.
fact: Recipes resembling macaroni and cheese appear in European cookbooks long before the dish became an emblem of American food.

name: Club sandwich
description: A layered sandwich of several slices of toast with chicken, bacon, lettuce, tomato and mayonnaise, usually cut into triangles and pinned with cocktail sticks. A fixture on the menu of American cafés and hotels.
fact: Where the "club" in the name came from is not certain; it is most often linked to private gentlemen's clubs.

name: Bagel with lox
description: A dense ring-shaped bagel, split in half, spread with cream cheese and topped with thinly sliced smoked or cured salmon. The dish is closely bound to the Jewish culinary tradition of New York.
fact: The habit of pairing a bagel with cream cheese and salmon took shape in the Jewish communities of New York around 1900.

name: Eggs Benedict
description: An English muffin with ham or bacon, a poached egg and hollandaise sauce, served hot for breakfast or brunch. There are several competing accounts of how the dish came about, all of them set in New York in the late nineteenth century.
fact: By one story it was put together for a regular at a restaurant who asked for something new to settle a hangover.

name: Pancakes
description: Fluffy pancakes from a batter raised with baking powder, fried in a pan and served in a stack with maple syrup and butter. A classic of the American breakfast, quite unlike thin crêpes in their porous, airy texture.
fact: The lift in American pancakes comes from baking powder in the batter, unlike thinner pancakes raised with yeast.

name: Belgian waffles
description: Thick waffles with deep pockets, particularly crisp outside and soft inside thanks to a yeasted batter. They are served with whipped cream, berries, chocolate sauce or a dusting of icing sugar.
fact: The deep pockets of Belgian waffles hold the topping well: syrup, berries or cream do not run off the surface.

name: Doughnuts
description: Rings or balls of enriched dough deep-fried and finished with glaze, icing sugar or sprinkles. One of the most recognisable desserts in the United States, with a whole chain of dedicated cafés grown up around it.
fact: The United States keeps an unofficial National Doughnut Day, observed since the 1930s.

name: Brownie
description: A dense chocolate cake with a moist, almost fudgy interior and a thin crust on top, often with nuts in it. The name comes from the brown colour of the bake and from its characteristic chocolate density.
fact: The ideal brownie sits between a cake and a biscuit; that in-between texture is the mark of a recipe that works.

name: Cheesecake
description: A dessert of cream cheese or curd on a biscuit base, either baked or set without heat, and often finished with a berry sauce. The modern American version, above all the New York style, has become the best known in the world.
fact: The simplest ancestors of cheesecake, curd desserts of a similar kind, existed in ancient Greece, long before the modern recipe.

name: Apple pie
description: An open or covered shortcrust pie filled with apple, cinnamon and sugar, and one of the chief emblems of American home cooking. The phrase "as American as apple pie" says everything about its standing in the country.
fact: Cultivated apple trees were brought to North America by European colonists; before that only wild species grew there.

name: Carrot cake
description: A spiced sponge built on grated carrot, nuts and warm spices, usually finished with a cream cheese frosting. The sweetness of the carrot and the richness of the frosting make this cake unusually moist and full-flavoured.
fact: Carrots were widely used in baking as far back as the Middle Ages, an affordable source of natural sweetness when sugar was dear.

name: Red velvet cake
description: A sponge cake of deep red colour with a faint cocoa flavour, usually layered with cream cheese frosting. The colour historically came from a reaction between cocoa and certain ingredients in the batter; today it usually comes from food dye.
fact: Much of its fame in the United States came from the restaurant at the Waldorf Astoria in New York, which served it as a signature dish.

name: Pavlova
description: A dessert on a meringue base, crisp outside and soft within, piled with whipped cream and fresh fruit, most often berries and kiwi. Named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, who toured Australia and New Zealand.
fact: Australia and New Zealand still argue with each other over which of the two countries invented this dessert.

name: Ice cream
description: A frozen sweet made from milk, cream or water with sugar and flavourings, known to humanity in one form or another for many centuries. There are dozens of kinds and techniques behind it, from gelato to soft serve.
fact: Ancestors of ice cream, frozen fruit mixtures made with snow and ice, existed in ancient civilisations long before refrigeration.

name: Caesar salad
description: A salad of romaine leaves, croutons and parmesan under a dressing of egg, garlic, anchovy and lemon juice. It was invented by a restaurateur of Italian origin working in Mexico, rather than in Italy or the United States.
fact: Legend has it the salad was thrown together from whatever was left in the restaurant kitchen once the main supplies ran out.

name: Greek salad
description: A salad of tomato, cucumber, red onion, olives and a thick slab of feta, dressed with olive oil. One of the great emblems of Greek cooking, recognisable at once by the bright vegetables set against the salty cheese.
fact: In Greece itself the dish is usually called the "village salad" rather than the Greek one.

name: Moussaka
description: A layered bake of aubergine, minced meat and béchamel sauce, browned on top in the oven. One of the central dishes of Greek cooking, though similar bakes turn up in the Balkans and the Middle East as well.
fact: The modern Greek recipe, with béchamel on top, took shape under clear French culinary influence in the early twentieth century.

name: Gyros
description: Meat roasted on a vertical spit, sliced thin and wrapped in a pitta with vegetables and tzatziki. The Greek counterpart of Turkish döner, and one of the most popular street foods in the country.
fact: The word gyros means "turn" or "circle" in Greek, after the way the meat rotates on the spit.

name: Ceviche
description: Raw fish or seafood marinated in lime or lemon juice with onion and chilli, the acid finishing the fish off without any heat. The dish is especially popular in Peru, considered one of the main places it came from.
fact: Citrus acid changes the protein structure in the fish much as heat does, which is why the flesh ends up looking cooked.

name: Empanadas
description: Pastry parcels filled with meat, cheese or vegetables, either baked or fried until golden. They are eaten all over Latin America and in Spain, and every country has its own fillings and its own shapes.
fact: In some Latin American countries the shape and the crimping of the edges tell you what the filling is before you bite in.

name: Feijoada
description: A thick stew of black beans with several cuts of pork and beef, traditionally served with rice, greens and orange slices. Regarded as the national dish of Brazil, and often cooked at the weekend as a reason to gather a crowd.
fact: In Brazil the custom is to serve feijoada on Saturdays, bringing family and friends together around the table.

name: Poutine
description: Chips buried under hot meat gravy and scattered with cheese curds, which soften slightly in the heat of the sauce. The dish comes from the Canadian province of Quebec, where it appeared in rural diners in the twentieth century.
fact: The name has nothing to do with any politician: it comes from a Québécois slang word for something like a mess.

name: Philly cheesesteak
description: A hot sandwich of thinly sliced beef and melted cheese in a long roll, invented in Philadelphia by street vendors who had been selling hot dogs. Today it is one of the city's emblems, and locals still argue over the right cheese: Cheez Whiz or provolone.
fact: Philadelphia has dozens of sandwich shops, each fiercely insisting that its own version is the real one.

name: Reuben sandwich
description: A layered sandwich of rye bread, corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and Thousand Island dressing, griddled until the outside crisps. Its invention is credited now to a New York restaurateur, now to one in Nebraska, both named Reuben, and the story is still argued over.
fact: Whatever the truth about its authorship, the sandwich has long been a classic of the American delicatessen menu.

name: BLT sandwich
description: A plain sandwich of bacon, lettuce and slices of tomato between two pieces of toasted bread, usually with mayonnaise. The name is simply the initials of the ingredients, and the combination is one of the most recognisable in American cooking.
fact: The abbreviation BLT, for bacon, lettuce and tomato, has stuck so firmly that menus rarely spell it out.

name: Peanut butter and jelly sandwich
description: Two slices of bread with peanut butter and fruit jam, the classic American school lunch, made in practically every household. The pairing of salty and sweet has turned it into one of the emblems of an American childhood.
fact: It is so familiar in the United States that people simply call it a PB&J, after the initials of the ingredients.

name: Po' boy
description: A Louisiana sandwich in a long, crackling roll, stuffed with fried shrimp, oysters, roast beef or whatever else is on offer. Legend ties the name to the words "poor boy", used for striking streetcar workers who were fed these for free.
fact: In Louisiana, ordering one "dressed" means it arrives with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise.

name: Sloppy joe
description: A bun heaped with loose minced meat in tomato sauce, which inevitably drips down your hands, hence the messy name. A cheap and simple dish that became a favourite in American school canteens and home kitchens alike.
fact: The word sloppy points to exactly the problem: eating one tidily is close to impossible.

name: Meatloaf
description: A loaf of minced meat, egg, breadcrumbs and spices baked in the oven, often glazed on top with tomato or ketchup sauce. A classic of American home cooking, and the sort of thing that belongs to a Sunday family dinner.
fact: The United States even keeps an unofficial National Meatloaf Day.

name: Cobb salad
description: A salad laid out in neat rows of chicken, bacon, egg, avocado, tomato and Roquefort on a bed of greens. Legend has it that it was put together in a Hollywood restaurant in the late 1930s, from whatever the kitchen had left.
fact: The salad is named after Bob Cobb, who owned the Brown Derby in Hollywood, where it was first served.

name: Waldorf salad
description: A salad of apple, celery, walnuts and mayonnaise, sometimes with grapes, invented at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in New York. Its crunch and its sweet, savoury flavour made it one of the emblems of American restaurant tradition.
fact: The original recipe had no nuts in it; they were added later, once the salad had become popular.

name: Chocolate chip cookies
description: Crumbly biscuits studded with pieces of chocolate, invented in the 1930s at the Toll House inn in Massachusetts. The recipe is said to have come about by accident, when the owner chopped a chocolate bar into the dough instead of using cocoa powder.
fact: The Toll House name stuck to the recipe: it is still printed on packets of Nestlé chocolate chips.

name: Pecan pie
description: A pie filled with pecans, eggs, sugar and syrup, which sets dense and chewy with caramel as it bakes. Especially popular in the American South, where the pecan trees grow, and traditionally served at Thanksgiving.
fact: The pecan is a close relative of the hickory, and its tree is the official state tree of Texas.

name: Pumpkin pie
description: A pie of spiced pumpkin purée with eggs, cinnamon and nutmeg, baked in a shortcrust shell. The unchanging dessert of the American Thanksgiving, standing for the harvest at the end of autumn.
fact: Most home-baked pumpkin pies in the United States are made not from fresh pumpkin but from ready-made tinned purée.

name: Key lime pie
description: A pie with a sweet-sharp filling of Florida key lime juice, condensed milk and egg yolks on a shortcrust or crumb base. It comes from the Florida Keys, and it is known for a bright yellow colour and a refreshing taste.
fact: A genuine key lime pie is never green: its natural colour is pale yellow.

name: Banana pudding
description: A layered dessert of vanilla custard, biscuits and slices of banana, left to stand in the fridge until the biscuits soften into cake. A classic of Southern American cooking, often brought out at family gatherings.
fact: For many years the recipe was printed straight onto the packet of Nilla Wafers vanilla biscuits.

name: Peach cobbler
description: A warm dessert of baked peaches under a layer of crumbly dough that bakes into a thick, irregular crust. The name cobbler catches the rough, patched look of the top, and the dish is especially loved in the American South.
fact: Cobblers arose among settlers who lacked the usual ingredients for a proper English pie.

name: Cornbread
description: A dense bread of cornmeal, baked in a skillet or a tin and served warm with butter. An inseparable part of Southern American cooking, and the usual companion to stews, greens and barbecue.
fact: Different regions of the United States argue over whether cornbread ought to be sweet or not.

name: Chicken pot pie
description: A covered pie filled with chicken, vegetables and a thick creamy sauce under a crisp pastry lid. This filling, homely dish became a symbol of comfortable American cooking and is often tied to family suppers.
fact: In English the phrase pot pie covers similar dishes with other fillings too, not only chicken.

name: Oatmeal cookies
description: Dense, crumbly biscuits made with rolled oats, often with raisins or cinnamon, baked until golden and crisp at the edges. They are regarded as the more wholesome alternative to a plain sweet biscuit, thanks to the fibre in the oats.
fact: Oatmeal cookie recipes spread across America largely thanks to cereal makers, who printed them on the packets.

name: Corn dog
description: A sausage on a stick, dipped in cornmeal batter and deep-fried until golden. A classic of American fairs and street festivals, eaten on the move, held by its wooden stick while the queue shuffles along.
fact: Hundreds of thousands of corn dogs are sold every year at the State Fair of Texas alone.

name: Onion rings
description: Rings of onion in a crisp coating, deep-fried to a golden brown, a popular side to burgers and steaks. They are on the menu of almost every American diner as the alternative to a portion of fries.
fact: Some diners make their onion rings from a single large onion, pulled apart into its separate layered rings.

name: Milkshake
description: A thick drink of milk, ice cream and syrup, whipped to a foam and usually served in a tall glass with a straw. It became an inseparable part of the American diner and the roadside café of the mid-twentieth century.
fact: The first milkshakes were made without ice cream: milk was simply whipped up with syrup and soda water.

name: Sundae
description: Scoops of ice cream under syrup or chocolate, finished with whipped cream, nuts and a cherry on top. Legend has it that the dessert appeared as a way around laws forbidding the sale of ice cream sodas on Sundays.
fact: Ithaca in New York State and Two Rivers in Wisconsin still argue over where the sundae was first served.

name: Banana split
description: A banana split lengthwise, with several scoops of different ice creams laid along it, plus syrup, whipped cream and nuts. One of the most recognisable desserts of the American ice cream parlour in the early twentieth century.
fact: The recipe is credited to a Pennsylvania pharmacist looking for a way to stand out from his competitors.

name: Baked beans
description: White beans slow-cooked in a sweet, spiced sauce with molasses or ketchup, often with pieces of bacon. The traditional side at an American barbecue or picnic, and especially widespread in the north-east of the country.
fact: Baked beans are so popular in Boston that the city earned the nickname Beantown.

name: Coleslaw
description: A salad of finely shredded cabbage and carrot in a mayonnaise or vinegar dressing, the compulsory side to barbecue and fried fish. The name comes from a Dutch word meaning cabbage salad.
fact: The recipe was brought to the United States by Dutch colonists as far back as the eighteenth century.

name: Pulled pork
description: Pork shoulder cooked slowly or smoked until it gives way completely, then pulled apart into strands by hand or with forks. It usually arrives in a bun with barbecue sauce, the basis of a sandwich across the American South.
fact: Making classic pulled pork in a smoker can take a full day and night.

name: Texas brisket
description: Beef brisket smoked over wood for hours on end, until a dense dark bark forms outside and the meat melts within. The calling card of Texan barbecue, with a whole competitive culture of pitmasters built around getting it right.
fact: Experienced pitmasters smoke a brisket for twelve to sixteen hours, aiming for the signature smoke ring under the bark.

name: Jambalaya
description: A Louisiana dish of rice cooked together with sausage, chicken or seafood, vegetables and Cajun or Creole spices. It was born from the mingling of French, Spanish and African cooking traditions in New Orleans.
fact: Jambalaya is considered a distant relative of Spanish paella, brought to Louisiana by colonists.

name: Grits
description: A porridge of coarsely ground corn, boiled to a creamy consistency and served at breakfast with butter, cheese or shrimp. One of the mainstays of the cooking of the American South, with roots in Native American recipes.
fact: The classic breakfast of shrimp and grits has become the calling card of coastal South Carolina cooking.

name: Clam chowder
description: A thick creamy soup of clams, potato and bacon, particularly popular in New England in the north-east of the United States. It is often served in a hollowed-out loaf of bread instead of a bowl, above all in San Francisco.
fact: New England has a running joke about a law forbidding tomatoes in a classic white chowder.

name: Crab cakes
description: Fried cakes of crab meat, breadcrumbs and spices, prized above all for the delicate sweetness of the crab itself. The dish is closely bound to the cooking of Maryland, where a particular species of crab is caught.
fact: In Maryland the best cakes are held to be those with more crab meat in them than breadcrumb and filler.

name: Lobster roll
description: A roll filled with pieces of boiled lobster meat dressed in mayonnaise or melted butter, the signature dish of the New England coast. The simplicity of the recipe lets the taste of the lobster come through in full.
fact: Maine and Connecticut keep two competing traditions: one with mayonnaise, the other with butter.

name: French toast
description: Slices of bread soaked in beaten egg and milk and fried in a pan until golden, served with syrup or berries. Despite the name, similar ways of using up stale bread existed in European cooking long before any French version.
fact: Dishes of bread soaked in egg have been known in Europe since the Middle Ages.

name: Hash browns
description: Grated or finely chopped potato fried in a pan until the crust turns crisp and golden, a compulsory part of an American breakfast. It comes either as a loose heap or pressed into a neat brick or patty.
fact: Fast food chains often press hash browns into a flat rectangular block, which makes them easier to serve.

name: Cinnamon roll
description: An enriched bun rolled into a spiral around butter, sugar and cinnamon, usually finished with sugar or cream cheese icing. The recipe came out of Scandinavian and German baking, but it found its greatest following in the United States.
fact: The smell of fresh cinnamon rolls became a signature marketing trick for the Cinnabon chain in shopping malls.

name: Funnel cake
description: Batter poured through a funnel into hot oil in thin streams, frying into a crisp lacy disc and dusted with icing sugar. A classic treat at American state fairs and amusement parks, eaten hot from the pan.
fact: The name funnel cake comes precisely from the funnel the batter is poured through into the oil.

name: Gumbo
description: A thick Louisiana soup built on a roux, with chicken, sausage or seafood, the "holy trinity" of vegetables and a load of spices. The dish draws together French, African, Spanish and Native American cooking traditions of New Orleans.
fact: The name probably goes back to a West African word for okra, one of the traditional ingredients.

name: Pastrami on rye
description: A sandwich of a thick layer of smoked, heavily spiced beef on rye bread, the calling card of the New York Jewish delicatessen. The meat is steamed for a long time before serving, which is what makes it so tender.
fact: In some New York delis the pile of pastrami in a single sandwich can weigh more than half a kilogram.

name: Mimosa salad
description: A layered salad of tinned fish, boiled eggs, cheese and onion under mayonnaise, with grated egg yolk scattered over the top. The crumbly yellow dust looks like mimosa blossom, which is where the name comes from.
fact: The name refers only to the look of the dish: there is no mimosa in it at all.

name: Crab salad
description: A salad of crab sticks, rice, sweetcorn, eggs and mayonnaise, which became one of the most popular festive dishes across the former Soviet Union in the 1990s. Despite the name, real crab meat almost never goes into it.
fact: Its popularity in the 1990s owed a great deal to the wide availability of cheap crab sticks.

name: Aspic
description: Pieces of meat, fish or tongue set in a clear jelly, made either with gelatine or with the natural setting power of cartilage. It is traditionally served cold on a festive table, very often at New Year.
fact: The clarity of the jelly is taken as a mark of the cook's skill: the stock for it is clarified long and carefully.

name: Rasstegai
description: An open pie of yeasted dough filled with fish or meat, with the top deliberately left ajar. The gap means that a little broth or melted butter can be poured in just before the pie reaches the table.
fact: The open top gave the pie its name, from the Russian verb meaning to unbutton.

name: Coulibiac
description: An oblong covered pie of yeasted dough with several layers of filling — fish, meat, cabbage, mushrooms or grain — separated by thin pancakes. One of the most ceremonial and laborious dishes in classical Russian cooking.
fact: French cooking took it up as coulibiac, most often made with salmon and rice.

name: Kutia
description: A sweet porridge of whole wheat grains or rice with honey, poppy seeds and raisins, made for funeral meals and for Christmas. Every ingredient carries a meaning, from the grain standing for life to the honey standing for plenty.
fact: At Christmas kutia is traditionally eaten first, opening the festive meal on Christmas Eve.

name: Kissel
description: A thick drink of berry or fruit juice set with starch, which can be either drinkable or dense enough to eat with a spoon. In early Rus it was made not from berries at all but from a brew of oats or rye.
fact: The old oat kissel set so firmly that it was cut with a knife and eaten in slices rather than drunk.

name: Kompot
description: A drink of fresh or dried fruit and berries boiled in sweetened water, a familiar part of lunch in homes and canteens across the former Soviet Union. It can be made from almost any seasonal fruit, from apples to dried apricots.
fact: In Soviet canteens kompot was almost always served as the obligatory third course of a set lunch.

name: Mors
description: A refreshing drink of pressed berry juice diluted with water and sweetened, most often made with cranberries or lingonberries. In Russian cooking mors was always thought of as good for a cold as well as good to drink.
fact: Unlike kompot, the berries are not boiled for long: the juice is pressed out and stirred into the brew at the end.

name: Kvass
description: A lightly fizzy drink fermented from rye bread or malt, with a distinctive sour edge to it. In summer it was traditionally sold from barrels right on the street, and it is the base of the cold soup okroshka.
fact: Natural fermentation leaves kvass barely alcoholic, around one per cent, which is why it counts as a soft drink.

name: Sbiten
description: A hot drink of honey and spices such as cinnamon, clove or ginger, drunk in Rus long before tea ever arrived. It was served as a warming winter drink, often at fairs, poured straight from a steaming urn.
fact: Street sellers called sbitenshchiki hawked it in the open air, carrying it in large copper vessels with a tap.

name: Medovukha
description: A lightly alcoholic drink of honey, water and yeast, sometimes with berries or spices, produced by natural fermentation. One of the oldest alcoholic drinks of the Slavs, and now enjoying a revival as part of historical cooking.
fact: In Russia medovukha has become the culinary souvenir of Suzdal, where it is brewed and sold to visitors.

name: Pastila
description: An airy sweet of whipped apple purée with sugar and egg white, dried to a light, paste-like texture. The pastila of Kolomna and Belyov is particularly famous, and making it to the old recipes has become a point of local pride.
fact: Traditional Belyov pastila is made from sharp, sour apple varieties, which give the sweet its especially delicate structure.

name: Zefir
description: A fluffy sweet of whipped fruit purée with sugar and a setting agent, which firms up into airy halves joined at their bases. It counts as the lighter relative of pastila and one of the most recognisable sweets of a Russian tea table.
fact: What holds zefir in shape is not gelatine but agar or pectin, and that is exactly why it stays so airy.

name: Tula gingerbread
description: A dense spiced biscuit filled with fruit paste and stamped with a pattern from a carved wooden mould, the culinary emblem of the city of Tula. The tradition of making them goes back centuries and is still alive in local bakeries.
fact: The pattern is cut into the wooden board in mirror image, so that it comes out the right way round on the finished biscuit.

name: Condensed milk
description: Sweet milk boiled down with sugar into a thick, sticky syrup, eaten on its own as a treat or stirred into baking and drinks. A tin of condensed milk with its blue and white label became one of the recognisable images of Soviet food culture.
fact: Boiled condensed milk, made by simmering the unopened tin for hours, became a popular treat in its own right.

name: Curd cheese bake
description: A baked mixture of curd cheese, eggs, semolina and sugar, often with raisins, which comes out firm outside and tender within. A familiar dish of nursery canteens and home breakfasts right across the former Soviet Union.
fact: The semolina goes in not for flavour but to help the curd mixture hold its shape while it bakes.

name: Vatrushka
description: A round enriched bun with an open middle filled with curd cheese, sometimes with raisins or jam. Simple, filling baking, traditionally served with tea, and still one of the most recognisable buns in Russian cooking.
fact: The shape of a vatrushka, raised at the rim with the filling open in the centre, goes back to old peasant baking.

name: Sharlotka
description: A plain sponge cake with apples, whose batter takes literally a few minutes to mix and in which the fruit makes up almost half the volume. The ease of the recipe makes it one of the most popular home desserts in Russian-speaking families.
fact: It differs sharply from the English charlotte: there is no bread and no jelly in it, only sponge and apples.

name: Kurnik
description: A tall covered pie with several layers of filling — chicken, rice, mushrooms and pancakes — traditionally decorated with shaped pastry on top. Such a pie was obligatory at Russian weddings, where it stood for prosperity and plenty.
fact: The name points straight at the chicken: without it a kurnik did not count as the real thing.

name: Rassolnik
description: A soup on meat or fish stock with pickled cucumbers, pearl barley and potato, which gives it a characteristic sour edge. One of the oldest Russian soups, and its name points straight at the cucumber brine in it.
fact: Its ancestor is reckoned to be the old kalya, a soup on cucumber brine made with fish or chicken.

name: Buckwheat kasha
description: Roasted buckwheat groats boiled until the grains stay separate and loose, traditionally served with butter, either on its own or as a side to meat. Buckwheat holds a place of its own in Russian cooking, among the best-loved of grains.
fact: Russia has historically been one of the world's largest producers and consumers of buckwheat.

name: Semolina porridge
description: A milk porridge of semolina, cooked down to a smooth, creamy consistency, the classic childhood breakfast in Russian-speaking families. Because of the risk of lumps, the grain goes in as a thin stream with constant stirring.
fact: Semolina comes from an intermediate stage of milling wheat, before the grain is ground down into fine flour.

name: Borodinsky bread
description: A dark rye bread with a distinctive sweet, spiced flavour of coriander and molasses, one of the most recognisable breads in Russia. Its dense crumb and deep aroma set it apart even among other rye loaves.
fact: Borodinsky bread is traditionally scattered on top with whole coriander or caraway seeds.

name: Salo
