description: Cured or smoked pork back fat, eaten in thin slices with bread, garlic and mustard. A particularly revered product of Ukrainian cooking, with a whole body of culinary traditions and jokes grown up around it.
fact: Ukraine holds entire festivals devoted to salo as a national product.

name: Sauerkraut
description: Shredded cabbage fermented in its own juice with salt, sometimes with carrot, apple or cranberries added. One of the oldest ways of putting vegetables by for the winter in Russian cooking, and valuable too for its vitamin C.
fact: Cabbage used to be fermented in large wooden barrels and shredded in a trough with a special curved chopper.

name: Pickled cucumbers
description: Cucumbers fermented or salted in brine with dill, garlic and leaves of horseradish or blackcurrant, until they take on their sour, salty taste. A traditional appetiser and winter preserve, and hard to imagine a Russian table without.
fact: The brine from pickled cucumbers has long been treated in folk tradition as a home remedy for a hangover.

name: Pickled mushrooms
description: Wild mushrooms boiled and covered in a marinade of vinegar, spices and bay leaf, a popular cold appetiser and a staple of the winter store cupboard. Gathering and putting up mushrooms has always been part of autumn life in Russia.
fact: The "quiet hunt", as mushroom picking is called, is still one of the most popular autumn pastimes in Russia.

name: Black caviar
description: Salted roe of sturgeon, prized for its delicate, buttery taste and large dark grains, and one of the most prestigious delicacies in the world. Overfishing has left the harvest strictly regulated, which has made it dearer still.
fact: Most of the black caviar on sale today comes from farmed sturgeon rather than fish caught at sea.

name: Red caviar
description: The roe of salmon species — pink, chum or sockeye — with large orange-red grains, a traditional delicacy of Far Eastern and festive Russian cooking. It is served on buttered bread or simply eaten by the spoonful.
fact: An open sandwich with red caviar became one of the chief emblems of the Russian New Year table.

name: Kartoshka cake
description: Sponge cake crumbled and worked together with butter and cocoa, then shaped into a potato and rolled in cocoa powder. A simple recipe made from leftover sponge, which is what made it one of the cheapest desserts in Soviet bakeries.
fact: Little dots of buttercream are often piped on top, playing up the resemblance to a real potato with its eyes.

name: Chak-chak
description: Pieces of deep-fried dough poured over with hot honey and pressed into a mound or some other shaped form. The great festive sweet of Tatar cooking, obligatory at weddings and celebrations of every kind.
fact: Kazan has a museum devoted to chak-chak, which also tells the story of the Tatar tea table.

name: Echpochmak
description: A triangular pie of unleavened dough filled with meat, potato and onion, into which broth is poured through a hole in the top before serving. Its three-cornered shape is also its name: echpochmak means triangle in Tatar.
fact: The filling never goes through a mincer: the meat and potato are cut into small cubes and go in raw.

name: Belyash
description: Round pies of yeasted dough with a meat filling, deep-fried with an opening left on top through which the meat shows. A dish of Turkic origin that spread right across Russia as a popular piece of fast food.
fact: The small hole on top of a belyash is left deliberately, so that excess steam can escape as it fries.

name: Pozharsky cutlets
description: Chopped chicken cutlets in a crisp coating of white bread, named after an innkeeper from the town of Torzhok. Legend has it that Nicholas I liked the recipe so much that the cutlets became famous across the whole country.
fact: The classic recipe puts butter into the mince and coats the cutlets in cubes of white bread rather than breadcrumbs.

name: Forshmak
description: A pâté-like appetiser of chopped herring, apple, onion and boiled egg, worked with butter into a smooth paste. The dish came out of Ashkenazi Jewish cooking and settled firmly into Russian and Ukrainian tradition.
fact: The name comes from a German word for a snack served ahead of the main meal.

name: Shurpa
description: A rich soup of lamb or beef with coarsely cut vegetables — carrot, potato and onion — seasoned with fragrant herbs. Widespread among Turkic and Caucasian peoples, and every region has its own version of the recipe.
fact: The vegetables are cut large and go in near the end of cooking, so that they do not fall apart in the broth.

name: Baursak
description: Small balls or diamonds of yeasted dough deep-fried to a golden, porous crust. A traditional treat of Kazakh and Central Asian cooking, served with tea and set out on the table at any celebration.
fact: At Kazakh celebrations a heap of baursaks is often piled on the dastarkhan as an obligatory offering to guests.

name: Kumis
description: A fermented drink of mare's milk, lightly fizzy and faintly alcoholic, produced by natural fermentation. The traditional drink of the nomadic peoples of the steppe, long valued for its supposed healing properties as well.
fact: In the nineteenth century kumis was used in dedicated sanatoria as a means of building up a patient's health.

name: Adjika
description: A hot paste of red pepper, garlic and herbs, made originally by Abkhazian shepherds as a seasoning for meat. Many versions of adjika exist today, including the milder tomato ones found all over the Caucasus.
fact: Classic Abkhazian adjika contains no tomato at all: it is purely a pepper and garlic paste.

name: Sulguni
description: A brined cheese with a dense, layered structure and a distinct sour-milk taste, made by a method close to that of mozzarella. It is served on its own as an appetiser and goes into baking too, notably Georgian khachapuri.
fact: The layered structure of sulguni comes from a particular technique of stretching the curd in hot water.

name: Pkhali
description: A cold appetiser of finely chopped vegetables — spinach, beetroot or beans — mixed with walnuts, garlic and herbs. The balls or little patties are often scattered with pomegranate seeds and served at the start of a Georgian meal.
fact: Pkhali is traditionally made from many different vegetables, so several kinds in different colours may appear at once.

name: Ajapsandali
description: A stewed vegetable dish of aubergine, pepper, tomato and onion with garlic and herbs, cooked without any meat. This plain, vivid Georgian dish is especially popular in the warm months, when the vegetables are at their best.
fact: For all its substance, ajapsandali is traditionally entirely vegetarian.

name: Currywurst
description: A fried pork sausage cut into pieces and doused in ketchup with curry powder, one of the most popular street snacks in Germany. The dish appeared in post-war Berlin and has been part of German fast food ever since.
fact: It was invented by a Berlin stallholder, Herta Heuwer, who mixed ketchup with curry powder in 1949.

name: Döner kebab
description: Thin slices of meat carved off a vertical spit, served in a flatbread or a wrap with vegetables and sauce. Turkish in origin, the dish found particular popularity in Germany, where it was reworked for quick eating on the street.
fact: In Germany the döner usually comes in a split flatbread, while in Turkey it is more often rolled in a thin wrap.

name: Croque monsieur
description: A hot sandwich of ham and melted Gruyère between two slices of bread, often finished under a layer of béchamel in the oven. A classic of French cafés, served both in bistros and at home as a quick supper.
fact: Put a fried egg on top and the sandwich becomes something else entirely: a croque madame.

name: Stollen
description: A dense Christmas loaf with dried fruit, nuts and spices, buried under a thick dusting of icing sugar. The tradition of baking stollen at Christmas in Germany goes back centuries and is strongest in the city of Dresden.
fact: Dresden holds an annual stollen festival, at which a giant festive loaf is baked and paraded.

name: Marzipan
description: A sweet paste of ground almonds and icing sugar, modelled into figures or used as a filling for sweets and baking. The marzipan of the German city of Lübeck is especially famous, and making it there became a local tradition.
fact: Marzipan brought Lübeck such fame that the city is called the unofficial capital of the sweet.

name: Mulled wine
description: Red wine warmed with spices — cinnamon, clove and citrus — and drunk at European Christmas markets through the cold months. The warm, spiced cup has become one of the chief emblems of the European winter holidays.
fact: The German name Glühwein means something like "glowing wine", after the heat it is served at.

name: Ayran
description: A fermented milk drink of yoghurt or kefir thinned with water and salted, widespread in the Caucasus and Central Asia. It is drunk in the heat as something refreshing and thirst-quenching, and often served with meat dishes.
fact: Similar drinks go by different names across the Turkic countries, though the recipe stays much the same.

name: Kefir
description: A fermented milk drink made with particular kefir grains, a symbiosis of bacteria and yeast. Legend has it that highlanders of the North Caucasus kept the recipe secret for a long time, and from there the drink spread across Russia.
fact: The yeast produces carbon dioxide and a trace of alcohol in kefir, which is why it prickles slightly on the tongue.

name: Ryazhenka
description: A fermented milk drink made from milk baked slowly in an oven and then cultured to a creamy consistency and a characteristic beige colour. This traditional Ukrainian and Russian drink is softer and creamier in taste than kefir.
fact: In village tradition the milk for ryazhenka sat for hours in a clay pot in the cooling oven.

name: Glazed curd bar
description: A bar of sweetened curd cheese with flavourings under a thin coat of chocolate glaze, a popular dairy dessert of the Soviet and post-Soviet food industry. Its compact shape and sweetness made it a favourite childhood treat for decades.
fact: Glazed curd bars like these are mass-produced not only in Russia but in Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia too.

name: Plombir
description: A dense dairy ice cream with a high milk fat content and very little air in it, which makes the flavour unusually rich. In the USSR plombir was made to one strict standard, so the taste was almost identical across the country.
fact: The name is linked to the French spa town of Plombières-les-Bains, where a similar dessert was made.

name: Tarkhun lemonade
description: A fizzy lemonade of bright green colour with the taste of tarragon, invented by a Georgian pharmacist as a tonic drink. Its unmistakable shade and herbal, peppery flavour make it easy to pick out among other Soviet soft drinks.
fact: The bright green shade comes from colouring: an infusion of tarragon gives nothing like it.

name: Duchesse lemonade
description: A fizzy lemonade with the taste of the duchesse pear, one of the most recognisable Soviet soft drinks alongside Tarkhun and Baikal. Its gentle sweetness and yellow colour kept it popular for decades on end.
fact: It was bottled to a single Soviet formula, and it is still produced in the countries of the former USSR.

name: Root beer
description: A fizzy drink with the distinctive taste of sassafras root and other herbs, made at first as a weak beer and later without any alcohol. Its peculiar medicinal flavour tends to divide anyone who did not grow up in the United States.
fact: Since safrole was banned, root beer has long been made not with real sassafras root but with flavourings.

name: Gogol-mogol
description: Egg yolks beaten with sugar, sometimes with milk or rum added, eaten with a spoon or drunk as a nourishing dessert. In folk tradition it was often used as a home remedy for a cold or a sore throat.
fact: A close relative of gogol-mogol is American eggnog: the same beaten yolks with sugar, milk and rum.

name: Calzone
description: A covered pie of pizza dough folded in half around a filling of cheese, ham and whatever else is at hand, then baked or fried. Essentially a pizza turned outside in, from Naples, and convenient to eat on the move.
fact: The name calzone can be translated from Italian as "trouser leg", after the pie's elongated shape.

name: Focaccia
description: A flat yeasted bread drenched in olive oil and scattered with coarse salt, rosemary or other herbs before it goes into the oven. The dimples pressed into the surface with the fingers are part of the traditional technique.
fact: In Liguria focaccia is eaten even at breakfast, with slices dipped straight into a cappuccino.

name: Panettone
description: A tall, enriched sweet loaf with dried and candied fruit, baked and eaten in Italy at Christmas. A long, slow fermentation of the dough makes the crumb remarkably light and airy for something of that size.
fact: A genuine Milanese panettone can take several days to make, because of the long fermentation of the dough.

name: Tortellini
description: Small rings of pasta filled with meat or cheese, folded by hand into their characteristic shape. Legend claims the shape was inspired by the navel of a beautiful woman, glimpsed by a cook through a keyhole.
fact: In Emilia-Romagna tortellini are served not with a sauce but in a strong meat broth: tortellini in brodo.

name: Pesto pasta
description: Pasta dressed with a sauce of basil, pine nuts, garlic, parmesan and olive oil, ground together into a fragrant green paste. The classic sauce comes from Genoa, where the local climate is said to make the basil especially aromatic.
fact: Traditional Genoese pesto is made by grinding the ingredients in a marble mortar with a wooden pestle, not in a blender.

name: Sachertorte
description: A chocolate sponge cake layered with apricot jam and coated in a dense chocolate glaze, created at the Sacher hotel in Vienna. The exact original recipe was fought over in court for years by rival confectioners claiming the "real" one.
fact: The first version was made in 1832 by a young pastry cook, Franz Sacher, working in the kitchen of Prince Metternich.

name: Tamales
description: Corn masa dough with a filling of meat, cheese or vegetables, wrapped in a corn husk or a banana leaf and steamed. A dish with centuries of history behind it, reaching back to the ancient civilisations of Mesoamerica.
fact: Before Christmas in Mexico tamales are made by whole families together, at gatherings called a tamalada.

name: Enchiladas
description: A corn tortilla rolled around a filling of meat or cheese, covered in hot chilli sauce and then baked. One of the staples of Mexican cooking, and it turns up in dozens of regional versions across the country.
fact: Different regions of Mexico make enchiladas with completely different sauces, from red to green to a meaty mole.

name: Haggis
description: A sheep's stomach stuffed with a mixture of offal, oatmeal, onion and spices, then simmered, the national dish of Scotland. It is traditionally served at a Burns supper on the birthday of Robert Burns, who wrote an ode to it.
fact: Because of a ban on sheep's lungs as food, genuine Scottish haggis could not be imported into the United States for years.

name: Yorkshire pudding
description: An airy bake of batter made from egg, flour and milk, cooked in scorching fat until it rises into a blistered dome. Traditionally served alongside the Sunday roast beef in a classic English dinner.
fact: Yorkshire pudding used to be served on its own before the main course, so that guests ate less of the expensive meat.

name: Victoria sponge
description: The classic English sponge cake of two layers sandwiched with jam and whipped cream, named after Queen Victoria. The simplicity and elegance of the recipe made it an inseparable part of the traditional English tea.
fact: The classic recipe is built on equal weights of butter, sugar, flour and eggs, which makes it easy to remember.

name: Avocado toast
description: A slice of toasted bread generously spread with mashed avocado, salt, pepper and lemon juice, often topped with a poached egg. The dish became a symbol of the modern coffee shop and of the fashionable breakfast of the 2010s.
fact: Avocados for toast have to be soft: the fruit is picked hard and only ripens after it has been harvested.

name: Irish stew
description: A rich stew of lamb or beef with potato, onion and carrot, simmered slowly until the meat gives way completely. A plain peasant dish that became the unofficial national dish of Ireland.
fact: The classic recipe is held to be so simple that on principle it contains no exotic spices at all.

name: Gingerbread man
description: A shaped gingerbread biscuit in the form of a little man, decorated with icing, tied by tradition to winter and Christmas holidays in Europe and the United States. Children know the figure from the tale of the gingerbread man who runs away.
fact: The dough is made dense, with honey or syrup and cinnamon and clove, so that the figure keeps its shape.

name: Crème caramel
description: A delicate egg custard baked in a water bath and turned out before serving, so that a layer of runny caramel sits on top. The dessert is found all over the world under different names, from the French flan to its Spanish and Latin American versions.
fact: The caramel goes into the bottom of the mould before the custard, and when it is turned out it runs down the dessert like a sauce.

name: Kulich
description: A tall, enriched cylindrical loaf with raisins and candied fruit under a cap of white icing, the great Easter bake of the Russian tradition. It is blessed in church along with the curd paskha and painted eggs before the festive meal.
fact: The dough is very rich, with a great deal of egg, butter and sugar in it, so it rises slowly and takes a long time.

name: Paskha
description: A dessert of sieved curd cheese, butter, sugar and dried fruit, pressed into the shape of a truncated pyramid in a special wooden mould. Its sides traditionally carry the symbols of Orthodox Easter: a cross and the initials of the greeting "Christ is Risen".
fact: Paskha is never baked: the curd mixture is left in its mould under a weight so that the excess moisture drains away.

name: Oladyi
description: Small, puffy pancakes of yeast or kefir batter, fried in a pan and served with sour cream, jam or honey. Thicker and fluffier than blini, they remain one of the most familiar options for a home breakfast.
fact: The batter is most often mixed with kefir and baking soda, which is what leaves them so porous inside.

name: Rice pudding
description: Rice simmered in milk with sugar and vanilla until it turns creamy, sometimes with raisins or cinnamon added. Desserts of rice and milk like this appear in the cooking of many countries under many different names.
fact: In Scandinavia it is a Christmas dish: one almond is hidden in the bowl, and whoever finds it is promised good luck.

name: Porridge
description: Porridge of rolled or whole oats boiled in water or milk to a soft, thick consistency, and one of the most widespread breakfasts in the world. In Scotland and England it has long been the foundation of a filling morning meal.
fact: Scotland holds official porridge-making competitions judged by the old rules.

name: Muesli
description: A mix of rolled oats, nuts and dried fruit eaten with milk or yoghurt, devised by a Swiss doctor as part of a healthy diet for his patients. Today it is one of the most common quick and wholesome breakfasts anywhere in the world.
fact: The recipe came from Dr Maximilian Bircher-Benner, which is why the original version is called Bircher muesli.

name: Granola
description: A mixture of oats, nuts and honey baked until crisp, eaten with milk, with yoghurt, or on its own as a snack. Devised at first as a health food, granola has become a staple of the modern wholesome diet.
fact: The name granola was fixed by John Harvey Kellogg, who worked at the Battle Creek sanatorium in America.

name: Smoothie
description: A thick drink of fruit, berries or vegetables whipped in a blender, sometimes with yoghurt or milk added. Smoothies took off sharply with the fashion for healthy eating and for something quick to consume on the move.
fact: The word smoothie comes from English and points to the even, smooth texture of the drink.

name: Chicken nuggets
description: Small pieces of chicken in a coating, deep-fried until crisp, and one of the mainstays of fast food all over the world. Their compact shape and versatility have made them particularly popular with children.
fact: The technique for nuggets made from ground chicken was developed in the 1960s by Robert Baker, a scientist at Cornell University.
